title: LangSmith BYOC is now available on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud
summary: LangSmith BYOC now runs on AWS (GA), Azure and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, and agent deployments stay in your cloud account while LangChain runs it.
story_key: story|title:langsmith byoc is now available on aws azure and google cloud
content_excerpt: LangSmith Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) now runs on AWS (GA), Azure (Beta), and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, datasets, prompts, and agent deployments stay in your own cloud account, on the cloud you choose, and LangChain manages the data plane for you, from orchestration and scaling to platform updates. You decide where your agents run and where your telemetry lives, without taking on the work of running LangSmith yourself. To make that possible, BYOC splits LangSmith in two. LangChain runs the control plane , which holds auth, org and workspace config, billing metadata, hashed API keys, and static UI assets. You own the data plane , which holds everything sensitive, from traces, prompts, and datasets to experiments, agent deployments, and workspace secrets. An organization can hold several data planes, each in its specific account and region, and each data plane holds its workspaces. This lets you split data planes by region, environment, or business unit. For example, a platform team might run production and staging data planes in separate AWS accounts, while a business unit that standardized on Azure runs its own, separate BYOC deployment on Azure. Each team's traces land in the account that team owns. Until now, teams with strict compliance boundaries deployed and maintained self-hosted LangSmith. This kept their data inside their own boundary, but it took dedicated platform engineers to patch stateful services, configure databases, and run schema migrations. With BYOC, LangChain provisions and operates LangSmith inside your own virtual network. Consider a team running agent applications across several environments. With self-hosted, every update to the execution components meant coordinating downtime and managing custom Helm rollouts in each environment. With BYOC, the data in your data plane stays in your VPC while LangChain handles scaling, schema updates, and runtime dependencies. Since we launched BYOC on AWS in August, many teams have chosen to run LangSmith in their own cloud with BYOC. They point to three main benefits: That demand is why we moved quickly to bring BYOC to Azure and Google Cloud, so teams can get access to this same experience on whichever cloud they run. Each cloud has its own network policies, identity model, and security requirements, so BYOC is built from each cloud's own building blocks. title: Why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
summary: Explore 3 principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows and how human-review is a strategic imperative for production-ready agents.
story_key: story|title:why human insight is a strategic advantage for building better agents
content_excerpt: As agents take on longer, more complex tasks, evaluating their performance means looking beyond the final AI-generated answer. Human review plays an important role in agent development: it helps teams define what good looks like, evaluate performance in context, and turn expert judgment into data that drives improvement. In this blog, we explore three principles for effective human-in-the-loop workflows: defining quality through expert judgment, evaluating agents in context, and turning human feedback into reusable evaluation data that drives continuous improvement. An agent trace is a record of everything an agent did in a single attempt: user messages, model responses, tool calls, and intermediate steps. Teams use traces to debug behavior, score quality, and decide what to fix. Often an engineer or an online evaluator flags a trace when something looks off. The flag is a signal, not an explanation. It usually is not enough to know how to change the agent. The flagged trace goes into an annotation queue . A human reviewer opens the interaction and leaves feedback: did the agent do the right thing, and why or why not? Automation chooses what to review. The human supplies the judgment that builders act on. In LangSmith , a queue item can be one run (a single step or span) or a thread (the full multi-turn session). With a thread, the reviewer sees the conversation the user had, instead of one step cut out of it. Each reviewer brings domain judgment the trace does not contain on its own: what “good” means in that job, what the user was trying to do, and what the agent should have done instead. This expert judgment is often highly specific to the company, role, or individual's expertise, and is a key part of building differentiated agents. Or as Snoop Dogg put it his commencement speech at CSU Long Beach : “Nobody can do you, like you do.” When a domain expert reviews a trace, one of the most valuable parts of the review is their reason. An expert can say why an output was right or wrong, and how a high-quality agent should behave. While reviewers can catch what automated evals miss, they also surface problems that sit beside the agent’s answer. For example, they might discover that an eval is scoring the wrong behavior, or that there is a gap in the rubric. One note in a queue can reveal a broader pattern worth fixing in the evaluator itself. This expert feedback changes the evaluations, and ultimately how the agent is built. title: Agent status in Paneflow: from screen rules to OSC 7501
story_key: story|title:agent status in paneflow from screen rules to osc 7501
content_excerpt: Since Paneflow 0.17.7 , the sidebar takes an agent's turn state from exactly one place: a status the agent writes into its own terminal. An agent that stops for a permission writes a sequence of this shape (the example comes from the spec): The usual assumption is that a tool running agents has to watch them from the outside: match the spinner, spot the permission prompt, notice the input box came back. I built that, several times, and deleted it. My position now is that the turn state belongs to the agent, the only process that actually knows it, and that the terminal's job is to carry the declaration without guessing. This is what ships in Paneflow 0.19.0. It covers the agents that emit OSC 7501: Claude Code from v2.1.295, and Codex, which merged support in openai/codex#52725 and #54114 in October. An agent that declares nothing gets no turn state, on purpose. The post follows one Claude Code turn from the agent to the sidebar, then the general shape, the six approaches that came before, what it costs, and the strongest objection. Mitchell Hashimoto published the Program Status Protocol on October 6, 2026, as "a completely generic, terminal-native specification" that came out of his work on Superlogical and Ghostty ( his post ). A program writes OSC 7501 with key=value pairs separated by colons: A program asks for support with OSC 7501 ; ? . There is no heartbeat. When the shell prompt returns ( OSC 133 A ) or the program exits, the terminal drops working and blocked ; done and error survive until the terminal decides to hide them, for example on the next keystroke. Two properties matter for Paneflow. The state comes from the one process that knows it. And the lifetime rules mean the terminal never has to time a state out. Let's follow a single turn through the three processes involved: the session host that owns the PTYs, the worker that reduces state, and the desktop window. Paneflow answers like Ghostty. The host starts every shell with TERM_PROGRAM=ghostty ( spawn_env.rs ), and its terminal engine is libghostty-vt . When Claude Code asks whether the terminal supports the protocol, the engine replies: The host sees that reply leave for the PTY and marks the session program_status_capable . Only the host answers. The desktop also embeds libghostty for drawing, but installs no OSC 7501 callback, so the agent never gets two replies; a test named desktop_terminals_neither_answer_nor_report_program_status keeps it that way. An agent can return a plausible answer while missing an important finding or reading the same source repeatedly. The answer alone won't explain why. Traces show the model and tool calls behind it, so you can investigate the failure, find related cases, and test whether a change helps. Databricks MLflow is now a supported destination for native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude Platform.. With native export to Databricks MLflow, developers using the Anthropic SDKs, the Messages API and Managed Agents can send native traces to Databricks and use MLflow to debug their agents and evaluate changes. MLflow Tracing is built on OpenTelemetry, an open standard for collecting and exporting service signals. A trace records an agent’s execution as individual steps, called spans, such as model requests and tool calls. Claude’s native instrumentation generates these spans and exports them using the OpenTelemetry Protocol. Databricks receives the spans through Zerobus Ingest and stores them in Unity Catalog tables linked to an MLflow experiment. You can inspect Claude traces alongside traces from other instrumented services, with the same tools for debugging and evaluation. Unity Catalog controls access to the data, which you can also query with SQL. With the combination of Zerobus and Unity Catalog, enterprises can get two crucial benefits: low-latency trace ingestion at high QPS plus the ability to govern access to the sensitive data stored in agentic traces. In Databricks, open the Experiments tab and click Create Experiment . Under Trace storage location , keep Unity Catalog selected. Choose an existing catalog and schema. This creates new MLflow experiments linked to the Unity Catalog table that stores OpenTelemetry traces. The detailed setup guide covers permissions and SQL warehouse requirements. title: Reimagining computational quantum research with AI scientists
summary: AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual Agents (RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally verified workflow repairs into such experience. RA substantially improves research performance under fixed base models and limited adaptation budgets. For example, RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash performance from 68% to 85%, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at a third of its cost despite using a weaker base model. We integrate all reproduced results into an extensible platform built on the model context protocol, making verified research workflows directly accessible to AI scientists and allowing new scientific papers to be continuously incorporated.

title: Optimize the Harness, Not the Model: Fitting a Minimal Agent to a Self-Hostable LLM for Investigative Analysis
summary: Government intelligence teams need LLM agents that can analyze large, messy evidence collections, but security and cost constraints often rule out hosted frontier models and broad, hard-to-audit tool surfaces. We report CLEO: Constrained Loop for Environment Optimization, a method for fitting a minimal agent harness to a fixed, self-hostable LLM. Given an expert-validated dataset, CLEO admits only the tools, guardrails, memory policies, and loop components that improve accuracy while remaining general and auditable. On our held-out dataset, the CLEO harness reaches an 83.8% pass rate, within 1.2 points of the strongest out-of-the-box Claude Code SDK baseline, while being two orders of magnitude smaller.

title: From Reactive to Agentic Resilience: Multi-Timescale AI-RAN Orchestration Under Signaling Storms
summary: Next-generation open radio access network (Open RAN) and AI-RAN deployments turn the RAN into a disaggregated, compute-aware platform whose service continuity depends on many control loops acting at different timescales. Resilience in this setting is best seen as a lifecycle spanning anticipation, absorption, adaptation, recovery, and evolution. Yet, existing mechanisms remain stage-specific and are rarely coordinated across the control hierarchy. This paper argues that agentic AI offers an orchestration layer that coordinates this lifecycle, turning operator intent into coordinated action while keeping slow language-model reasoning off the fast control path. Using mass-attachment signaling storms as a running study, we build a discrete-event Open RAN attach simulator that captures retry amplification, shared-compute contention, and non-instantaneous provisioning, and we propose a three-tier framework in which an orchestrator at the service management and orchestration layer sets a standing policy, a per-site non-real-time agent judges storms and anticipates scheduled crowds, and a deterministic near-real-time loop enforces every decision. Across experiments, the agentic controller approaches the resilience of a fully provisioned pool of servers at a quarter of its capacity by reading a scheduled event from a calendar and provisioning ahead of it. No reactive weight setting recovers this once the surge arrives. Free-text operator intents ground into control directives at 94% exact match on previously unseen intents, and a single instruction reshapes live behavior end to end. We also quantify the latency, cost, and contention limits that bound it. The supplementary material provides analytical proof of the derived Theorem on anticipation horizon, as well as the subsequent Corollary results on reactive provisioning limits.

title: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language
story_key: story|variant:small|title:palette teaching a small model to build decks in your design language
content_excerpt: Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other. Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it. A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at. It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from. It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent. There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them. Nobody makes a deck in one pass. title: Why Agents Are Soon Only Going to Have 1 Tool
summary: Instead of triggering tools one at a time across turns, agents are collapsing their tool catalog into a single exec(code) tool—chaining, filtering, and awaiting actions inside an isolated sandbox.
story_key: story|title:why agents are soon only going to have 1 tool
content_excerpt: For the past two years, building capable Agents meant designing tools, figuring out which actions help the model complete a task, deciding how granular each tool schema needs to be, or iterating on system instruction templates. This is changing. Agents are moving in the opposite direction by collapsing their entire tool catalog into one tool : exec . This is called Code Mode (or Programmatic Tool Calling). Instead of forcing the model to trigger tools one at a time across turns, the harness gives the model a single exec(code) tool. The model writes a short TypeScript or Python script that chains, combines, and awaits actions inside an isolated sandbox. To understand why agents are converging on a single exec tool, we should look at how tool calling evolved. Initially, we only gave agents a handful of tools because they couldn't reliably choose or filter across a large catalog. As models improved, we connected dozens of tools or MCP servers, but ran into context window limits. We solved that with tool search and progressive disclosure , letting agents look up tools on demand. Even with dynamic tool loading, we still had dozens of individual tools, and were still stuck with the limitation of standard tool calling: one action per turn. In standard tool calling, the model generates a structured object (typically JSON) that defines a single action (or at best a flat batch of independent calls, like reading three files), waits for the raw output to come back, adds it into the prompt history, reasons again, and decides what to do next. From my own experience, we made a big jump recently in how reliably models can combine and chain dependent actions in a single pass: Several shifts came together to enable this. Frontier models are trained heavily on code, and providers have started post-training models for Code Mode. At the same time, MCP servers now increasingly ship outputSchema alongside inputSchema , giving the model upfront knowledge of return types so it can chain Tool A into Tool B inside the same script before seeing runtime output. Code Mode collapses the tool catalog into a single tool on the model surface: exec(code) . Instead of passing 80 separate JSON Schema tool objects to the model API, the agent compiles those schemas into compact type declarations ( declare namespace tools { ... } ). When the model needs to combine actions across external systems, it calls exec and writes a script that invokes await tools.<server>.<tool>(args) . To save context a

title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.

title: claude-code v2.1.316
summary:
What's changed

  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_ULTRATHINK, which turns the ultrathink keyword off
  • Added pooled group budgets to the Claude apps gateway: one monthly budget that a group's members share, on top of each member's own limit, set with pooled_budget on the spend limits admin API
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_LOOPED_CROSS_CERT_DROP to keep system cross-certificates that certify each other in a loop, for servers whose private CA needs one
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_EFFORT to set the effort level subagents run at when nothing else names one, instead of inheriting the session's
  • Added managed.policy_mode: layered to the Claude apps gateway: every policy that matches a developer applies, each merged over the ones listed below it, not only the first
  • Added guardrail.input_tagging on Claude apps gateway Bedrock upstreams, which wraps prompts in the input tags that an Amazon Bedrock guardrail's prompt attacks filter needs; all_messages_and_system also tags the system prompt
  • Deprecated fast mode for Opus 4.8 as of October 30, 2026; it will be removed on November 30, 2026. After removal, fast mode requests on Opus 4.8 return an error and do not fall back to standard Opus 4.8. Migrate to Opus 5.5 to keep the speedup
  • Fixed shell commands being left running on macOS and Linux when Claude Code exits by itself, for example when credentials are refused or a cloud session is archived
  • Fixed bash aliases with line breaks in their value (except in Git Bash), and functions whose names start with a dash, being garbled or lost in the Bash tool's shell
  • Fixed bash scripts started from the Bash tool stopping after their first command when SHELLOPTS is exported
  • Fixed PowerShell hooks not blocking on exit code 2 when the command begins with a type cast, param, using or an attribute
  • Fixed some network requests hanging when a compressed response was cut off or corrupted
  • Fixed sonnet, opus and haiku on Vertex AI and Amazon Bedrock showing an error mid-session instead of switching to an older model when the newest is not yet available to the account or region
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway not checking every model a request names against availableModels, deniedModels and models; a request that names a blocked model now gets a 400 naming the field
  • Fixed claude auth login refusing to run where managed settings require a Claude apps gateway; in a terminal it now shows the gateway sign-in
  • Fixed --restricted sessions uploading files from outside the working directories when a Read allow rule covered them
  • Fixed prompts containing invisible characters needing a second Enter to send; plain prompts now send cleaned on the first Enter, and commands still wait for review
  • Fixed sub-agents that inherited a parent sub-agent's model moving to the main model when a background job or message woke them
  • Fixed a managed autoMode.allow list without "$defaults" getting the built-in exceptions back from a host app's --settings, a first rule added in /permissions, or /auto-mode-setup
  • Fixed cloud sessions and cloud scheduled tasks not being marked as failed when auto mode stopped a turn because the server returned no safety verdict
  • Fixed claude -p text output sometimes not saying why auto mode stopped a turn when a background agent was still running
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1 being ignored in sessions started by a host application (such as Claude Desktop) behind a proxy or LLM gateway with experimental betas turned off
  • Fixed plugin MCP headersHelper scripts receiving a corrupted CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT and server URL when a credential-named environment variable was set to a switch value such as 1
  • Fixed the SDK register_repo_root control request not loading the CLAUDE.md of a directory outside the working directory (with CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1)
  • Fixed the Artifact tool showing ? for artifact database access rules at the self level, and not quoting those rules back when it refuses a republish that would drop them
  • Fixed /model <id> not warning when the model isn't recognized by this version and auto-compact will assume a 200K context window
  • Fixed the "hold space to speak" hint using up its three showings in one session, and showing an empty key when push-to-talk is unbound
  • Fixed Grep and Glob never returning when the search process is killed at the timeout but does not exit, seen on Windows
  • Fixed a rare case where resuming a conversation did not restore its plan, when /clear or /resume had been run while part of that conversation was still being saved
  • Fixed first-run setup dropping words from the security notes and the terminal-setup explanation in narrow terminals
  • Fixed the Enterprise survey card taking a typed 1 or 0 after a short pause; a typed answer now needs Enter
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a message sent while Claude was working being answered after a Stop, once the session's process had been replaced
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an MCP server's on/off switch sometimes being lost when a session moved to a new machine
  • Windows: Fixed the Bash tool losing your aliases and functions in Git Bash when the rc file sets errexit and pipefail and only winpty aliases, or none, are defined
  • Improved /code-review started from the Code tab in Claude Desktop or on the web: cloud and claude remote-control sessions now show the findings card, not a plain-text list
  • Improved /diff on large repositories: each refresh usually runs one fewer full-repository git command, and refreshes are spaced out when git is slow
  • Improved the messages shown when /ultrareview, a cloud session or a cloud agent finds no GitHub remote: they now say to create a repository at https://github.com/new, and /ultrareview no longer suggests a gh command that gh rejects
  • Improved SSL certificate errors to name the likely causes, among them a server that leaves out an intermediate certificate, and the fix for each
  • Changed auto mode so that an autoMode.allow list without "$defaults" no longer removes the built-in rule on scheduled-task prompts
  • Changed server-managed settings for Team and Enterprise logins: settings fetched from Anthropic's API now apply without an approval prompt, and a stored copy that doesn't verify is refused
  • [VSCode] Added sign-in to a Claude apps gateway from the chat panel, with no terminal needed
  • [VSCode] Changed ultrathink to run its turn at xhigh effort and show in a rainbow in the chat box, as in the terminal
  • [VSCode] Fixed the missing Effort slider, Ultracode switch and model name when the model setting has the [1m] tag, such as opus[1m]
  • [VSCode] Fixed saved /btw side-question history being deleted too early while a settings file has errors
  • [VSCode] Fixed a conversation coming back in Auto mode after a reload or restart when its plan was approved with "Yes, and manually approve edits"
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a form card to cloud sessions, so you can fill in or decline a form an MCP server asks for instead of the request being canceled without you seeing it
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a "Catching up…" line that shows while a cloud or Remote Control session you switch back to is still bringing its messages up to date
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed network secrets so Enterprise members can add and delete them on their own cloud environments, instead of only viewing them
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the Changes pane for cloud sessions: the note about what the list leaves out is now a badge beside the branch name, not a row above the diff
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed file search in a cloud session's Files pane showing folders as ../.. paths after Claude changed directory; results now show their path from the project's root
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude refusing to edit or append to a canvas it made in a Slack channel, from that channel, once the canvas was also shared to another channel or a DM
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed untagged replies going unanswered in a Slack Connect thread when both organizations have installed Claude and Slack delivered the reply to the other organization's app
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a cloud scheduled task's live status checklist in Slack staying half-done; a run can now edit the top-level messages it posted during that run
  • [Claude Tag] Changed a Slack channel's Respond automatically switch to a "How Claude participates" choice on the channel's Configure page and in Claude Tag admin settings
  • [Code Review] Added a findings-by-severity card to the Code Review analytics page, showing the period's total findings, a daily chart stacked by severity, and each severity's count
